text: PodSecurityPolicy used to be Kubernetes' built-in way to restrict what a Pod's spec could contain — no privileged containers, no running as root. It worked, but policies were matched to Pods through RBAC bindings in a confusing way, and a wrong binding could silently leave workloads unprotected. It was deprecated in 1.21 and removed in 1.25. What replaced it is simpler: three predefined profiles called the Pod Security Standards.

Privileged is fully unrestricted, reserved for the system and infrastructure workloads that genuinely need that access. Baseline blocks the most obviously dangerous settings while staying compatible with most normal workloads — no privileged containers, no host namespaces, no mounting sensitive host paths. Restricted layers on top of that: containers must run as a non-root user, privilege escalation must be disabled, Linux capabilities must be dropped by default, and a seccomp profile has to be set.

Since Kubernetes 1.25, Pod Security Admission enforces these standards automatically — it's a built-in admission controller, on by default, with nothing extra to install. It reads three possible labels on a namespace: enforce, which actually rejects a violating Pod; audit, which lets it through but logs the violation; and warn, which lets it through but prints a warning to the client. That three-level split is what makes a safe rollout possible.

The namespace label only enforces what's already in the Pod spec — you still have to write a securityContext that satisfies it. runAsNonRoot refuses to start any container that would run as UID zero. allowPrivilegeEscalation set to false closes off setuid-style escalation. Dropping all capabilities strips every Linux capability by default, so you add back only the one a container genuinely needs. Read-only root filesystem isn't part of the standard, but it's a cheap addition — a compromised process can't write a payload to disk with nowhere to write it.

Rolling restricted onto a namespace that's already running workloads doesn't mean flipping enforce and hoping nothing breaks. Set warn and audit to restricted first and watch what would have failed without blocking a single Pod. Fix whatever the audit log flags, then flip enforce once you're actually confident — turning a potentially disruptive change into a measured one.

Pod Security Admission covers exactly three fixed profiles, with no concept of organization-specific rules like requiring images from one internal registry. That's when a cluster reaches for a dedicated policy engine — OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno — plugged in as an admission webhook alongside PSA, not instead of it. Next lesson moves up a level, from what's inside the cluster to the control plane protecting it: the API server and etcd themselves.
